title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at median gross rent across counties in New York, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Choosing what to measure

my_state <- "NY"        # two-letter abbreviation, in quotes
my_variable <- "B25064_001"     # the variable code, in quotes

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York        1252     22  315374    NA
2 36003 Allegany County, New York       754     33   47027    NA
3 36005 Bronx County, New York         1436     11 1419250    NA
4 36007 Broome County, New York         914     26  197738    NA
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York    759     30   76479    NA
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York         895     39   75464    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         51        381479.
2 Moderate                11         37898.


[High-confidence counties have an average population of approximately 381,479, while moderate-confidence counties have an average population of approximately 37,898. No counties fall into the low-confidence category under these thresholds. This pattern suggests that more populous counties tend to have more reliable median gross rent estimates than less populous counties.]

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
1.Among New York counties, we know the least about housing costs in Hamilton County, which has the largest relative margins of error at approximately 11.05%. In addition, Schuyler County, Greene County and Lewis County have high margin of error, at 8.74%, 7.96% and 7.19%, which showes that madian gross rent is not accurate for these countries. 2. This pattern occurs because the ACS is based on a sample rather than a complete count of every resident. Smaller counties get fewer responses. So according to our math knowledge, Its results are less accurate. 3. If we assume that every piece of data is highly accurate, then these very small counties might receive too much or too little funding, leading to either overspending or underspending—which could result in wasted funds or people not receiving sufficient assistance. Rural counties with very small populations, such as Hamilton County, are particularly vulnerable.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
The article by Alfred Lubrano (2018) compares poverty rates in Philadelphia between the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 American Community Survey (ACS) five-year estimates. Because the article does not identify the census tracts that make up each informal neighborhood, I analyze poverty at the census-tract level instead of trying to reproduce its neighborhood values exactly.
I use ACS table B17001, Poverty Status in the Past 12 Months by Sex by Age. B17001_001 is the population for whom poverty status is determined, and B17001_002 is the number of people below the poverty level. The poverty rate is therefore B17001_002 / B17001_001. I use ACS 5-year estimates because the article uses them and they are available for census tracts. The periods do not overlap: they cover 2006–2010 and 2013–2017. Each figure nevertheless pools five years of survey responses rather than representing a single-year count.


Show code
poverty_vars <- c(
  poverty_universe = "B17001_001",
  below_poverty = "B17001_002"
)

philly_2010 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  variables = poverty_vars,
  year = 2010,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

philly_2017 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  variables = poverty_vars,
  year = 2017,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 2 — Test

Calculate rates, margins of error, and reliability


Show code
tract_2010 <- philly_2010 |>
  transmute(
    GEOID,
    tract = NAME,
    universe_2010 = poverty_universeE,
    universe_moe_2010 = poverty_universeM,
    poverty_2010 = below_povertyE,
    poverty_count_moe_2010 = below_povertyM
  )

tract_2017 <- philly_2017 |>
  transmute(
    GEOID,
    universe_2017 = poverty_universeE,
    universe_moe_2017 = poverty_universeM,
    poverty_2017 = below_povertyE,
    poverty_count_moe_2017 = below_povertyM
  )

tract_poverty <- tract_2010 |>
  inner_join(tract_2017, by = "GEOID") |>
  mutate(
    rate_2010 = poverty_2010 / universe_2010,
    rate_moe_2010 = moe_prop(
      poverty_2010, universe_2010,
      poverty_count_moe_2010, universe_moe_2010
    ),
    rate_2017 = poverty_2017 / universe_2017,
    rate_moe_2017 = moe_prop(
      poverty_2017, universe_2017,
      poverty_count_moe_2017, universe_moe_2017
    ),
    # ACS MOEs use a 90% confidence level, so divide by 1.645 to obtain SE.
    cv_2010 = (rate_moe_2010 / 1.645) / rate_2010 * 100,
    cv_2017 = (rate_moe_2017 / 1.645) / rate_2017 * 100,
    reliability_2010 = case_when(
      cv_2010 < 12 ~ "● Reliable",
      cv_2010 <= 40 ~ "▲ Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE ~ "✖ Unreliable"
    ),
    reliability_2017 = case_when(
      cv_2017 < 12 ~ "● Reliable",
      cv_2017 <= 40 ~ "▲ Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE ~ "✖ Unreliable"
    ),
    change = rate_2017 - rate_2010,
    change_moe = sqrt(rate_moe_2010^2 + rate_moe_2017^2),
    statistically_detectable = abs(change) > change_moe
  )

# A zero poverty universe means a poverty rate and its CV are undefined.
missing_tracts <- tract_poverty |>
  filter(is.na(rate_2010) | is.na(rate_2017))

analytic_tracts <- tract_poverty |>
  filter(!is.na(rate_2010), !is.na(rate_2017))


Eight tracts have an undefined rate in at least one period. In each case, the ACS poverty universe is zero in at least one year; these are nonresidential or otherwise very low-population areas, not evidence of a zero poverty rate. I exclude them from rate, reliability, and change calculations because a ratio with a zero denominator is undefined. This leaves 376 tracts for analysis.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 3 — Adjudicate
The article’s statement that Philadelphia had about a 26% poverty rate in the 2013–17 ACS is supported: aggregating the tract estimates gives a rate of about 25.8%, which rounds to 26%. The tract-level evidence also supports the more limited statement that some Philadelphia places experienced measurable changes in estimated poverty rates. Thirty-six tracts had statistically detectable increases, while 27 had detectable decreases.
The broad suggestion that poverty rose robustly throughout Philadelphia is not supported by this tract-level test: 313 of 376 usable tracts have changes that are not distinguishable from zero at 90% confidence. The article’s exact claims about Fairhill, Eastwick, and Holmesburg cannot be determined from this analysis. Those places are informal neighborhoods, and the article does not publish the tract-to-neighborhood boundaries it used. The Holmesburg claim also requires a separate analysis of poverty among White residents, which is not measured by the all-resident poverty rate used here.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 4 — Rewrite
New five-year Census estimates show that poverty remained widespread in Philadelphia in 2013–17, when about 25.8% of residents with a determined poverty status were below the federal poverty line. At the census-tract level, some places saw statistically detectable changes from 2006–10: 36 tracts had estimated increases and 27 had decreases. In most tracts, however, the estimated change was not distinguishable from sampling error at the 90% confidence level. The data point to uneven change across the city, but they do not by themselves establish the article’s exact claims about informal neighborhoods such as Eastwick or Holmesburg.
